samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers name the specific problem behaviors and propose autosave, removing the unit-change confirmation, safer reset handling, and checks after release. B goes further: new hives copy settings from an existing hive, an Essentials/Advanced split separates common from rare settings without removing any, and a settings-only reset can be undone. A is tighter and handles the risks well, but it lacks copy-from-hive and is less explicit about demoting rarely used settings. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers handle the save model, the unit-change confirmation and the reset button well, and both name the specific problem behaviors. B gives sharper post-release metrics and a clearer staged rollout, but lacks copy-from-existing-hive and never says outright that no options are removed.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers address every concrete problem and propose similar fixes. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend explicit modes and back it with situation-specific reasoning. B gives a sharper concrete variant: Select is a safe, read-only resting state, Paint is a hold-to-paint quasimode, and Record is a button that always shows its target cue. B also adds overwrite-specific confirmation and cue version history. A is thorough and argues fairly for the other camp's speed advantage, but its safeguards are more generic, and it keeps Record as a full mode without questioning that choice. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers firmly reject the timing-based gesture model and protect against show-time mistakes with visible mode indicators, undo for paint, a confirm before overwriting a cue, and a show lock. A comes out slightly ahead because it treats Record as a separate button rather than a mode and offers hold-to-paint, which ends the mode when the finger lifts. That makes mode errors structurally less likely, not just better signalled. B is thorough and fairly credits the other camp's speed argument, but some of its points, such as accessibility and general touch imprecision, are more generic.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend the same variant: Select as the default, Paint as an explicit and visible tool, and Record as a separate button. A goes further on show-time safety: painted lights show their new values, Undo shows how many lights changed, the target cue number is on the Record button, and it argues for keeping cue versions so the operator can undo instead of confirming. B is tighter and gives a frank account of mode errors, but it is less concrete. It also overstates a wrong paint as changing all 48 lights. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the same recommendation: Select as the default, Paint as a visible mode, and Record as a separate button rather than a mode. Both explain clearly why the timing-based gestures are risky. B goes further on show-time safety: it shows the mode and the painted values on the grid itself because the operator's eyes are there, counts the lights changed so a runaway drag is obvious, prints the target cue on the Record button, and suggests keeping cue versions instead of a confirm step. B's accessibility and screen-reader points are more generic. A openly admits that modes cause their own errors, but its plan to drop out of Paint after every stroke would slow down an operator who paints repeatedly.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make the same core recommendation: Select as the default mode, Paint as a separate armed mode, and Record as a button rather than a mode. A gives more show-relevant detail: an indicator that doesn't depend on color alone in a dim booth, each paint stroke as one undo step, a Record button that shows the cue number and asks for a cue-specific confirmation before overwriting, a rehearsal test with deliberate distractions, and an open question about whether paint changes the stage immediately. B is shorter and adds a useful show-lock idea, and it names the cost of switching modes more directly, but its indicator and undo guidance are less specific. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reach the same sound design: Select as the default, Paint as an armed tool that is clearly shown on screen, and Record as a separate button that asks for confirmation. Both also explain clearly why the timing-based gesture option fails. B is stronger on show-time safety: it says not to rely on color alone in a dim booth, gives every action a route that doesn't need a gesture, and puts status in a fixed bar. It also ties its strictness to whether painting changes the stage immediately or only edits a preview. A is tighter but less thorough.
